meta.title: Who really said "Success is going from failure to failure without losing your enthusiasm"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Churchill. This popular line is an anonymous saying first documented in 1953; Churchill scholars find it nowhere in his canon. The real, hedged story.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success is going from failure to failure without losing your enthusiasm'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Churchill and not Lincoln. An anonymous saying first traced to 1953, misattributed decades later. Here is the documented provenance.

answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — an anonymous saying
answer.sourceLine: This line is found nowhere in Churchill’s writings or speeches. Quote Investigator traces the earliest close matches to anonymous sources in 1953; the Churchill attribution only appears decades later with no citation, and roughly as many sources wrongly credit Abraham Lincoln.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Winston Churchill (and, almost as often, Abraham Lincoln)
How to Say a Few Words (David Guy Powers, 1953)

source.excerpt: Success has been defined as the ability to go from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.
trail: The earliest close match found by Quote Investigator is a 1953 public-speaking guide, How to Say a Few Words by David Guy Powers, which presents the line anonymously as a definition of success.
The International Churchill Society lists it among quotes falsely attributed to Churchill: “We can find no attribution… broadly attributed to Winston Churchill.”
Churchill bibliographer Richard Langworth confirms it is “found nowhere in his canon,” and notes an almost equal number of sources credit Abraham Lincoln with no attribution either.
Quote Investigator found further anonymous 1950s–60s variants (“advancing from failure to failure,” “staggering from failure to failure”) before the Churchill misattribution took hold in the 1980s.
source.excerptNote: The 1953 wording recorded by Quote Investigator — presented as a definition “success has been defined as…,” with no author claimed.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: full investigation of this saying

source.rightsNote: The exact wording has no identifiable author: the earliest documented instances (1953) are anonymous, so no copyright or public-domain status can be responsibly asserted for the phrase itself. (The 1953 book How to Say a Few Words in which it is recorded is a separate, later work and does not claim the line.)

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British statesman, orator & author · the quote is misattributed to him
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill was Britain’s wartime Prime Minister and a Nobel laureate in Literature whose vast, meticulously documented output makes fabricated “Churchill” quotes easy to catch. Despite his fame as a phrasemaker, this saying appears in none of his works — it is listed among the “Red Herrings” of false attributions by his own editors and biographers.

cite.sourceCitation: Anonymous, quoted in David Guy Powers, How to Say a Few Words (New York: Doubleday, 1953); earliest documented instance per Garson O’Toole, Quote Investigator, “Success Is Going from Failure to Failure Without Losing Your Enthusiasm,” 28 June 2014.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Success is going from failure to failure without losing your enthusiasm’?” Last verified 16 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: Anonymous saying (earliest documented 1953); popularly misattributed to Winston Churchill

misattribution.heading: How Churchill got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” misattribution: an anonymous mid-century aphorism that migrated onto a famous orator once it was too good to leave unsigned.

items.why: Credited to Churchill across posters, LinkedIn and quote sites, but it appears in none of his speeches or books. The International Churchill Society and bibliographer Richard Langworth both find no attribution.
Roughly as many sources pin it on Lincoln — also with no citation. Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence for either man.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented versions, from 1953 onward, are anonymous; the saying has no known author — see Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Churchill
lead: Churchill is one of the internet’s biggest quote magnets: pithy, resilient-sounding lines gravitate to him because, as Quote Investigator puts it, statements “appear to be more forceful and memorable when linked to major orators.” A definition of success built on cheerful persistence is exactly the register people expect from him — which is precisely why it was so easy to misassign.
In reality the phrase surfaced anonymously in 1950s American self-improvement and public-speaking writing and drifted through several wordings before the Churchill label stuck in the 1980s.
context.pull: An anonymous 1953 definition — not a Churchill line.
